summary: Considers how Differentiated Services interacts with IP tunnels of various forms. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An IP tunnel wraps a packet in a second IP header, which creates two Diffserv markings. This memo explains when a tunnel should use the inner marking and when it should use the outer one.

questions: what is diffserv over a tunnel
uniform model vs pipe model diffserv
does dscp copy to the outer ip header
subtitle: How to handle the two DSCP values created when an IP tunnel wraps a packet.

tldr.problem: An IP tunnel adds an outer IP header, so the packet can carry two DSCP markings, while the Diffserv architecture provided incomplete guidance on how to use them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes uniform and pipe models, places conditioning before or around encapsulation, and recommends statically selecting the inner or outer DSCP at egress.
tldr.outcome: The Informational memo gives tunnel designers guidance on preserving Diffserv behavior. It says IPsec tunnel egress must select the inner DSCP unless an adequate security analysis supports another choice.

today: RFC 2983 is an Informational memo that discusses Diffserv behavior for IP tunnels. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Tunnels and Two DSCP Values
sections.content:
An IP tunnel adds an outer IP header to the original packet's inner IP header. Intermediate nodes normally inspect and may change only the outer header, including its Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP). At egress, the outer header is removed.

The RFC treats tunnels as unidirectional and considers IP tunnels. It says the Diffserv architecture did not provide enough guidance about how the two DSCP values should relate. It recommends describing the behavior a tunnel must preserve rather than requiring one fixed outer per-hop behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunneled packet has an inner header for the original traffic and an outer header for the tunnel. Routers inside the tunnel generally use the outer DSCP.

sections.title: Uniform and Pipe Models
sections.content:
In the uniform model, the tunnel is treated as part of the end-to-end path. The sender copies the DSCP to the outer header during encapsulation, and the receiver copies the outer DSCP back to the inner header during decapsulation.

In the pipe model, the tunnel hides the intermediate nodes from end-to-end conditioning. The egress uses the inner DSCP and discards the outer value. If the ingress and egress are in different Diffserv domains, the egress may need to condition traffic for its domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The uniform model carries the outer marking back into the inner header. The pipe model keeps the inner marking and ignores the outer one when the packet exits.

sections.title: Where to Condition Traffic
sections.content:
The memo recommends placing Diffserv traffic conditioning in series with tunnel encapsulation rather than adding a parallel path. At ingress, conditioning can happen before encapsulation or on the outer header. Conditioning the inner header is difficult because it requires reaching inside a packet.

For encrypted or integrity-protected tunnels such as IPsec, changing the inner header is not possible. If a DS-incapable egress discards the outer header, the ingress may need to set an inner DSCP compatible with the egress network. Tunnels sensitive to packet reordering may need traffic marked as one ordered aggregate.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic can be conditioned before a packet is wrapped or on its outer header. Changing an encrypted or integrity-protected inner header is not possible.

sections.title: Choosing a DSCP at Egress
sections.content:
Decapsulation reduces two DSCP values to one. Making both values available to later conditioning would add complexity, so tunnels should support a static choice of either the inner or outer DSCP at egress. The outer DSCP usually carries the useful information for a uniform-model tunnel; the inner usually does for a pipe-model tunnel.

IPsec tunnels usually use the pipe model and are required to select the inner DSCP for security reasons. The memo says not to select the outer DSCP without an adequate security analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: At the tunnel exit, the design should choose in advance whether to keep the inner or outer DSCP. IPsec tunnels are required to use the inner value under the guidance in this RFC.

sections.title: Security at Tunnel Egress
sections.content:
Diffserv security considerations still apply when traffic passes through a tunnel. An egress node inside a Diffserv domain acts as an ingress node for traffic leaving the tunnel and must condition traffic to address theft-of-service and denial-of-service threats.

For IPsec, the outer header is discarded unless the traffic conditioning to be applied is known and has been analyzed for security vulnerabilities. This restriction applies to conditioning at the tunnel egress.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel exit must check traffic before it enters its Diffserv domain. IPsec requires discarding the outer header unless the planned handling has been assessed for security risks.
